grade.why: Pictured: 2 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

kind.note: Whistler's index no. 1, 'Block Houses', drawn at the north-west and south-east angles; Quaife: 'Two blockhouses ... stood at the northwestern and southeastern corners of the quadrangle'.

construction.note: Not stated. Timber, like every building of the post except the magazine, which Quaife singles out as brick.

stories.note: Not stated on the sheet. The folded elevation draws a building of more than one storey, and a blockhouse that commands the space between two picket rows fires from above them.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. Two storeys of log, the second fort's blockhouse figure; the folded elevations are not to scale.

upper_overhang_m.note: Unattested. The jettied upper storey is what the type is; its size is a typical one.

loopholes.note: Whistler's index lists '2 Port Holes for Cannon' and '3 Loop Holes for small arms' among the fort's features, and Quaife (after Wilson) puts the fort's cannon in the blockhouses. The register could not locate either numeral, so the slits' pattern and height are the archetype's.

roof_type.note: Unattested. A four-sided pitched cap over a near-square plan is the surviving type. Whistler's index adds 'the Cupolas are not yet built on the Block Houses as laid down'; the cupola that now stands at the apex is in `cupola`, with its own confidence, rather than folded into this attribute (T-3041).

chimneys.note: T-3041 picture refinement. Kurz & Allison (1893), panel 1, draws each first-fort blockhouse with a roof lantern and no separate chimney. The former one-stack value was an unattested heating reconstruction; removing that invented stack follows the pictured silhouette without asserting that a retrospective print proves historical absence. The lantern itself and the panel's conflicting tower locations remain unresolved; no plan, bearing or documented 75 ft flagstaff is changed. The complete 1812 total (including possible hidden fittings or schematic omissions) remains reconstructed; this is a conservative model choice to follow visible evidence, not positive proof of the historical total or absence. Source-visible counts remain explicit.

cupola.note: PLANNED IN 1808 AND PICTURED AFTER; NEVER DATED (T-3041, owner adoption 2026-11-03, T-3335). Whistler's 1808 draught lays the cupolas down on both blockhouses and its index says they were 'not yet built ... as laid down', so they were intended and not yet standing then. Kurz & Allison (1893) panel 1 draws a small roof lantern on each first-fort blockhouse and no stack, and Currey's 1912 bird's-eye (after the 1899 Tribune sketch of Van den Berghen's 1898 model) draws a small square body under its own pyramid cap on both. Intent plus two later depictions is what carries INFERRED that they were finished before the fort burned in August 1812; no source dates their completion, both pictures are tier-5 retrospectives, and Whistler's note is kept as the counter-evidence for the years before. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED and none is in this record: the side, the height, the cap's pitch and eave and the plain boarded sides are the fort_structure archetype's cupola kit (the second fort's, T-2388), reused at the proportions both pictures show, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L-first-fort-blockhouse-cupolas-3041 owns them. No louvres, glazing or finial is built.

cupola_construction.note: T-3041, the owner's reading of the pictures (2026-11-07): the cupola is laid in log like the rest of the blockhouse, not boarded. Currey's bird's-eye draws the cupola bodies with the same horizontal courses as the walls below them, and a garrison building its blockhouses in log would raise the lookout on top the same way. Course height, notching and chinking are the blockhouse's own (coursed log wall, L370); nothing in the pictures measures them.

cupola_height_m.note: T-3041: the body from its seat in the main roof to the cap's eave. The owner (2026-11-07), comparing the first build with the fort's drawings: the cupolas read about 20% too tall. The kit's 2.1 m body is cut to 1.6 m, which makes the whole cupola (body above the roof plus cap) about 20% shorter. Neither picture is to scale; this is a proportion read by eye, recorded in docs/LIBERTIES.md L-first-fort-blockhouse-cupolas-3041.

cupola_ports.note: T-3041, the owner's reading of Currey's bird's-eye (2026-11-07): each face of the cupola's cap carries a small dark opening, a lookout to see far off. The drawing shows two faces of each cap with one opening apiece; the other two faces are taken to match. It is too small to give the openings' shape or size, so each is built as a small framed opening under a shed hood, its width, height and place on the face reconstructed (fort_structure_params CUPOLA_PORT_*; docs/LIBERTIES.md L-first-fort-blockhouse-cupolas-3041).

function.note: The north-west of the first fort's two blockhouses. Quaife (after Wilson): one held two small cannon and the other one; which is which is not said, and no gun is built.

placement.position_note: SEATED WITH ONE ORIGIN AND ONE BEARING FOR ALL FOURTEEN (T-2050), so no building moves against another. The box is the register's (data/traces/whistler_1808_fort_dearborn.json), read off the commandant's own measured draught at 4.52 px per foot from the 75 ft staff, good to about +/-1.1 ft an edge. THE ORIGIN: the staff's foot, which the register finds at the centre of the parade and within about a foot of the centre of both picket rows, is set on the fort site at local E +1152, N +221 - the Wright 1834 reading of the fort's place that docs/ROADMAP.md S5a cross-checks to 35 m against the modern landmark. That is the SITE, not the second fort's plan: John H. Kinzie (quoted on chicagology_prefire052) says the first fort 'stood upon the same ground as the last Fort' and 'was differently constructed', so the place carries over and nothing of the 1816 geometry does. THE BEARING: the frame's north is set on grid north, which is the register's own inference that the sheet's right is east, from the lake lettered down that margin; the sheet has no north arrow, so the bearing is inferred and adds nothing to it. The second fort's 8 degrees, read off Harrison 1830, is that fort's and is not borrowed. Grid and true north differ here by under half a degree. A CHECK, NOT A FIT: seated so, the outward row's west side stands about 124 ft from the 1812 river (data/terrain/epochs/e1830_natural/river.geojson) and the north-west blockhouse about 65 ft from it; the draught's red-ink '122 feet to River' from the west side and Wilson's '80 feet' from the north-west corner are figures of that size. Carry the datum's +/-20 m on the whole frame.
placement.symbolic_location: First Fort Dearborn, in the frame of Whistler's 1808 draught (register part 'north-west blockhouse'): E -55.8..-38.5 ft, N +40.3..+59.3 ft of the flagstaff's foot, square to the curtains, straddling the angle of both picket rows. SEATED (T-2050) with the whole frame: the staff's foot at local E +1152.0, N +221.0, the frame's north on grid north; this record's origin is the box's SW corner.
